meta.title: Beyond the Desert: Stories of people and discoveries
meta.description: Temporary exhibition at Biblioteca Salaborsa, Bologna.

hero.lead: Step into a land where ancient worlds meet cutting-edge science. From vast deserts to thriving civilizations, discover how archaeology is uncovering the past — and helping us understand the climate challenges of our future.

library.title: Library
library.lead: The Reading Room — books, e-books and a film on Arabia, selected for the exhibition and held at Biblioteca Salaborsa.

geography.title: Geography
geography.lead: Decades of Italian and international archaeological work mapped across the Arabian Peninsula — from Yemeni highlands to the Omani coast.

history.title: Stories of People and Discoveries
history.lead: The Arabian Peninsula has always been a space of adaptation and relation between Africa, Asia, and the Mediterranean — shaped by water, metals, oases, and trade routes.

prehistory.title: Prehistory
prehistory.body:
As early as the Paleolithic, over 700,000 years ago, the Arabian Peninsula was crossed and inhabited by human groups moving between Africa and Eurasia. Their presence was not continuous: climatic oscillations turned territories that are arid today into landscapes of lakes, watercourses, grasslands, and wildlife, while the return of aridity reduced settlement and prompted communities to reorganize routes and strategies.

In the Neolithic, between ten thousand and six thousand years ago, hunting, fishing, and gathering were integrated with the herding of sheep, goats, and cattle. Rather than the sedentary agricultural village typical of the Near East, the communities of Arabia adopted flexible strategies, combining herding, hunting, fishing, gathering, and seasonal mobility according to the opportunities offered by coasts, terraces, foothills, and mountains.

bronze.title: Bronze Age
bronze.body:
In the third millennium BCE, copper made the Arabian Peninsula a protagonist of the great trade networks of the Near East. Mesopotamian sources name the land of Magan — southeastern Arabia and the Oman Peninsula — and the kingdom of Dilmun in the Gulf.

Copper was an engine of exchange, connecting Mesopotamia, Iran, the Indus Valley, the Arabian Gulf, and the Sea of Oman. Plants and agricultural practices circulated too, contributing to the formation of the oasis. Water, date palms, cultivation, and herding built more stable productive landscapes without erasing seasonal mobility.

iron.title: Iron Age & Late Antiquity
iron.body:
In the first millennium BCE, water and mobility became decisive forces. In southeastern Arabia the falaj spread — tunnels and channels tapping underground water toward fields and oases — favoring agriculture, denser settlement, and connections between mountains, plains, and coasts.

The domestication of the dromedary transformed desert travel. The South Arabian Kingdoms, including Saba, prospered on irrigated agriculture, caravan routes, and the trade of frankincense and myrrh, while the north and northwest linked the southern routes to the Levant and Rome.

preIslamic.title: Islamic Period
preIslamic.body:
In the seventh century CE, the birth of Islam deeply transformed the Peninsula. Mecca and Medina became the centers of a new religious and political community, uniting diverse groups without erasing local traditions.

Even when power shifted outside Arabia, the region kept an essential role: the holy cities remained poles of pilgrimage, and the coasts continued to take part in the trade of the Red Sea, the Arabian Gulf, and the Indian Ocean.

research.title: UniBo Excavations in Arabia
research.lead: Decades of University of Bologna archaeological research in Oman — from the Joint Hadd Project to ongoing missions at Ras Al-Hadd, Al-Khutm, Halban, and Romail.

rasAlHadd.title: Ras Al-Hadd
rasAlHadd.lead: Bronze Age coastal landscape around the HD-6 settlement and the HD-7/HD-10 necropolises, investigated by the University of Bologna for over thirty years.

khutm.title: Al-Khutm
khutm.lead: Part of the UNESCO area of Bat, Al-Khutm & Al-Ayn, where the University of Bologna joined the excavation of a monumental circular stone platform, conventionally called a 'tower'.

halban.title: Halban Necropolis
halban.lead: Monumental Bronze Age tombs on a limestone terrace in Al-Batinah, excavated since 2023 with digital survey, osteoarchaeology, and isotopic analysis.

romail.title: Romail Shelter
romail.lead: A prehistoric rock shelter between the Wahiba Sands and the Hajar Mountains, documenting the transition from Final Paleolithic to Neolithic about 10,000 years ago.

history.title: Forty years in Oman
history.lead: From Maurizio Tosi's first campaigns at Ras Al-Hamra in the late 1970s to today's DiSCi and DBC projects, Bologna's archaeologists have shaped how the prehistory and protohistory of southeastern Arabia are understood.

references.title: Scientific References
references.lead: Selected scholarly sources underpinning the exhibition's panels and research.

climate.title: Climate, Oases and Aflaj
climate.lead: In Arabia, water was the decisive element. Communities transformed arid environments into productive oases and, from the Iron Age, built the falaj irrigation systems — five of them inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in Oman.

aflaj.title: The Aflaj of Oman
aflaj.body: A falaj (plural: aflaj) is a hydraulic system that captures water from springs, water tables, or aquifers and carries it by gravity to settlements, palm groves, and fields. The water is divided into shares and shifts under community management. Introduced at the beginning of the Iron Age along the foothills of the Al-Hajar Mountains, thousands of aflaj are still documented in Oman today, and five are inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
aflaj.unesco: UNESCO World Heritage: Aflaj Irrigation Systems of Oman (2006)

climate.title: Water in an arid land
climate.body: In the popular imagination the desert is empty and hostile, yet Arabia's history is far more complex. Its communities did not merely cross arid environments — they learned to know them, exploit their resources, and, in some cases, transform them into productive landscapes. Collecting, conserving, distributing, and protecting water demanded technical knowledge, social organization, and a continuous capacity for adaptation.

archive3d.title: 3D Archive
archive3d.lead: Rotate, zoom, and place burial structures from Ras Al-Hadd and Halban in your own space using augmented reality. Scan QR codes in the exhibition to view in AR.
